title: Reconciliation: can I come back?
hook: the fear of mortal sin keeps people away for years; the sacrament of return is a door, not a wall

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Eucharist, source and summit. Your line was everything flows from the table. Did you thank someone out loud? Day one hundred twenty-nine.

A text at one in the morning, typed and deleted three times, to the one friend who still goes to Mass. Is it true I can't come back until I confess? I haven't been in six years. Am I in mortal sin? Do I have to fix everything first? The friend isn't sure either. So the question goes back in the drawer, and another year goes by. A lot of people carry some version of that text. It deserves a straight answer, and a kind one. Today: reconciliation.
screen: `A TEXT AT 1 A.M.` → `AM I IN MORTAL SIN?` → `A STRAIGHT ANSWER, AND A KIND ONE.`

segments.voice: First, what the Church actually teaches, without softening it. The Catechism says that skipping Sunday Mass on purpose, with no serious reason, is a grave matter. Being sick, caring for someone, or being somewhere with no Mass within reach is not a sin at all. And for any sin to be mortal, three things must all be true at once: grave matter, full knowledge, and deliberate consent. We'll go deeper on that later in the year. Then the Catechism adds a line worth remembering: we can judge that an act is wrong, but the judgment of persons belongs to God alone. Nobody gets to pronounce a verdict on your soul from the parking lot. Not even you. Second, what to actually do. Mass is open; you can go this Sunday. If there may be serious sin, Catholics wait on Communion and go to confession first. That isn't a fee at the door. It is the door. The sacrament's name says so. Reconciliation, from the Latin reconciliare: to bring together again. Jesus tells of a son who wastes everything and walks home with a speech rehearsed. In the Douay-Rheims: "when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and running to him fell upon his neck, and kissed him." The father runs before the speech is done. Third, when the fear won't let go. Some people confess, hear the words of forgiveness, and still can't believe it. They check and recheck every thought for sin. Catholic spiritual writers have an old name for this: scrupulosity. The Church meets it gently. A steady confessor helps, and so can a good counselor; it isn't a lack of faith. Fourth, the feeling afterward. Some walk out in tears of relief. Some feel awkward, or nothing at all. Catholics believe the forgiveness is just as real either way.
screen: `WHAT MAKES A SIN MORTAL: ALL THREE.` · `MASS IS OPEN. CONFESSION IS THE DOOR.` · `SCRUPULOSITY: WHEN FEAR WON'T LET GO.` · `FORGIVEN, FELT OR NOT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be met on the road. Settle, and breathe. Picture a long road home, and yourself on it, going over what you'd say. Now picture someone far off at the end of it, who has already seen you, and is already running. Don't finish the speech. Let yourself be met halfway. If there's something you've been carrying, let it come along as it is. If you pray, you can hand it to God in a word. The bell holds the time.
Reconciliation. From the Latin for bringing back together. The sacrament of return, where Catholics confess to a priest and hear that they're forgiven: a door, not a wall. Today's word.
Your line: there's always a way back. Today, take one small step toward someone you're at odds with. A message, a smile, a hello. Day one hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics who have been away can return to Mass at any time; those aware of serious sin go to confession before receiving Communion. Many parishes offer confession on Saturday afternoons, and priests are used to hearing 'it's been a long time, and I don't remember how.'

myth: you have to go to confession before you're allowed back into Mass
Mass is open to anyone. confession comes before receiving Communion, if there may be serious sin.
missing Mass because you were sick is a sin
a serious reason, like illness or caring for someone, excuses it.
Catholics believe forgiveness in confession is real even if you feel nothing
the sacrament doesn't depend on the feeling afterward.

fork.setup: you're the father. your son who left and spent everything is walking up the road, a great way off, rehearsing a speech. what do you do?
options: wait on the porch for his apology.
run to him, embrace him and kiss him.
send a servant to ask what he wants.
fork.reveal: he runs. "moved with compassion, and running to him fell upon his neck, and kissed him." the speech hardly gets started.

original.note: Latin: to bring together again, to restore; from re- and conciliare, to bring together.

trapdoor: what you thought: if you've missed Mass for years, you're locked out until you've fixed everything.
what it means: the door is open. Mass is open now, and confession is the way back to the table, not a toll before the door.
what a scholar hears: CCC 1857 requires grave matter, full knowledge and deliberate consent together, and CCC 1861 leaves the judgment of persons to God alone.

SENSITIVE (mortal sin): the lesson must not loosen moral teaching. It states CCC 2181 plainly (deliberately missing Sunday Mass without serious reason is grave matter) and the three conditions (CCC 1857), then CCC 1861 (judgment of persons belongs to God). Keeper: confirm 'Nobody gets to pronounce a verdict on your soul from the parking lot. Not even you.' reads as faithful to CCC 1861 and not as a dismissal of conscience.
'Being somewhere with no Mass within reach is not a sin at all': based on canon 1248 §2 and CCC 2181 (serious reason / impossibility). Confirm wording.
Scrupulosity: described pastorally; 'a good counselor' is mentioned because scrupulosity can overlap with OCD. Confirm.
Mortal and venial sin are taught in depth on day 311; 'we'll go deeper on that later in the year' points there.
